title: Topology-dependent mixing of knots in flexible polymer chains
abstract: The organization of multiple knots along a polymer contour can depend sensitively on the topology of the constituent knots. Using coarse-grained Brownian-dynamics simulations, we investigate topology-dependent mixing of two knots in a flexible polymer at controlled normalized wall separation. We compare homogeneous ($3_1\otimes 3_1$) and heterogeneous ($3_1\otimes 5_1$) knot pairs using a contour-based coordinate that distinguishes mixed and demixed configurations. Starting from partially overlapping configurations, the $3_1\otimes 5_1$ pair is observed in mixed configurations more frequently over the simulation time window than the $3_1\otimes 3_1$ pair at intermediate wall separation. We further find that, over the intermediate range of normalized wall separation, mixing of the $3_1\otimes5_1$ pair produces a composite knotted region that occupies substantially less polymer contour than the two constituent knots collectively occupy in demixed configurations. The corresponding reduction in contour occupancy is much smaller for the $3_1\otimes3_1$ pair. This indicates that the heterogeneous constituent topologies can be accommodated within a smaller portion of the polymer contour in the composite configuration. These results establish that constituent topology can strongly influence multiple-knot organization in flexible polymers.
summary: This work simulates the organization of multiple knots on a flexible polymer chain, comparing homogeneous and heterogeneous knot pairs. The simulations reveal that the constituent knot topology strongly dictates the system's tendency to mix or remain separated. Specifically, the heterogeneous pair exhibits enhanced mixing and a structural advantage by occupying less contour space when interpenetrated.
main_problem: The study investigates how the inherent topology of multiple knots influences their organization (mixing vs. demixing) within a flexible polymer chain.
main_result: Heterogeneous knot pairs ($3_1 \otimes 5_1$) show a greater tendency to mix and achieve a composite state that occupies less polymer contour than the constituent knots separatedly, compared to homogeneous pairs ($3_1 \otimes 3_1$).
method: Coarse-grained Brownian-dynamics simulations are employed to track the time evolution and probability distribution of the knot configuration.
model_or_system: The system is a flexible polymer chain confined between two opposing walls, modeled using a potential energy function including bond, excluded volume (WCA), and wall potentials.
key_observables: Relative frequency of mixed vs. demixed configurations, contour occupancy reduction upon mixing ($\Delta L$), and the boundary-based knot-separation coordinate ($\Delta b$).
important_parameters: Normalized wall separation ($x = d/L$) and the specific topologies of the constituent knots ($3_1$ and $5_1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on coarse-grained dynamics and uses a boundary-based metric ($\Delta b$) to classify topological states, which is assumed to be robust.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate probability distributions of the knot separation coordinate ($\Delta b$) versus wall separation ($x$), and show how the contour occupancy reduction ($\Delta L$) differs between the two knot pairs.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the statistical sampling of mixed versus demixed states for two knot pairs ($3_1 \otimes 3_1$ vs. $3_1 \otimes 5_1$) across varying wall separations, focusing on the structural consequences of mixing.
why_interesting: The findings provide insights into how topological constraints can mediate non-trivial collective behavior in complex polymeric systems, which has parallels in understanding entanglement or topological defects in quantum many-body systems.

Figure 1: Schematic definition of the contour-based knot-separation coordinate ∆b. Orange and green markers denote the starting and terminal beads, respectively. (a) In a demixed configuration, the localized knot regions are separated along the polymer contour, and ∆b = b(s) 2 −b(t) 1 > 0 gives the contour gap between them. (b) In a fully mixed configuration, the outer boundaries define a composite knotted region, while one constituent knot is independently localized within it. In this case, ∆b = b(s) comp −b(t) nest < 0, and |∆b| provides a boundary-based measure of nesting rather than an overlap length between two independently localized constituent intervals.

Figure 4: Color maps of the probability distributions of the contour-based knot-separation coordinate as a function of normalized wall separation x for (a) 31 ⊗31 and (b) 31 ⊗51. Positive ∆b corresponds to non-overlapping knot regions, whereas negative ∆b reflects overlap or nesting. Both systems exhibit distinct positive-∆b and negative-∆b branches whose relative statistical weights vary with normalized end separation. The 31 ⊗31 pair shows greater sampled statistical weight in the demixed branch, while the negative-∆b branch is comparatively more pronounced for 31 ⊗51 at intermediate normalized separation.
